title: How an agent team runs a multi-day coding mission
subtitle: One orchestrator plans, fresh workers build one feature at a time, and validators who never saw the code check it.
hook: Done is defined before any code, and features run one at a time: parallel workers fought.

sources.title: The Multi-Agent Architecture That Actually Ships
sources.speaker: Luke Alvoeiro

nodes.label: You
nodes.detail: You describe a goal, scope it in a conversation with the orchestrator, and approve the plan. Then the system runs for hours or days and you can do something else.
nodes.tradeoff: The bottleneck is human attention, not model intelligence; a five-person team on 10 work streams might handle 30.

nodes.label: Orchestrator
nodes.detail: Acts as a sounding board, asks strategic questions, and produces a plan of features, milestones and a validation contract. At milestone boundaries it reviews handoffs and scopes follow-up work.
nodes.tradeoff: Its logic is about 700 lines of prompts and skills, not a hard-coded state machine, so it improves with each model.

nodes.label: Validation contract
nodes.detail: Written during planning, before any code, it defines correctness independently of the implementation. Each feature gets one or more assertions, and together the features cover all of them.
nodes.tradeoff: Large projects can need hundreds of assertions, but tests written after the code only confirm decisions, not catch bugs.

nodes.label: Shared mission state
nodes.detail: State every agent references, carrying the plan, shared constraints and the skills the orchestrator writes for each mission's workers.
nodes.tradeoff: It uses primitives models already know, like agents.md and skills, so the deterministic code stays thin.

nodes.label: Worker
nodes.detail: Gets one feature with clean context and no accumulated baggage, reads its spec and implements it. Read-only jobs like code search or API research run as parallel sub-agents.
nodes.tradeoff: Only one worker or validator runs at a time; slower on paper, but the error rate drops dramatically.

nodes.label: Git repo
nodes.detail: Each worker commits its feature to Git, so the next worker inherits a clean slate and a working codebase.
nodes.tradeoff: Running many writers in parallel failed: agents stepped on each other's changes and duplicated work.

nodes.label: Structured handoff
nodes.detail: A finished worker fills in what it completed and left undone, the commands it ran with exit codes, issues found, and whether it followed procedure.
nodes.tradeoff: Progress is blocked until handoff issues are addressed, so the mission self-heals instead of relying on agents remembering.

nodes.label: Scrutiny validator
nodes.detail: Runs after each milestone: the test suite, type checking and lints, plus a dedicated code review agent for each completed feature.
nodes.tradeoff: It has never seen the code before, so it is not invested in the implementation and reviews adversarially.

nodes.label: User testing validator
nodes.detail: Acts like a QA engineer: launches the app and, through computer use, fills forms, clicks buttons and checks that flows work end to end.
nodes.tradeoff: It takes much longer than scrutiny; most of a mission's wall-clock time is spent here, not generating tokens.

flow.text: You describe a goal, argue scope, then approve the plan.
Plans features and milestones, and writes the validation contract before code.
A fresh worker reads its spec, builds one feature, commits to Git.
Worker records what is done, undone, commands run and exit codes.
At the milestone: tests, type checks, lints, one review agent per feature.
Launches the app and clicks through real flows like a QA engineer.
Reads handoffs and results, then scopes follow-up features to fix gaps.

takeaways.text: Define what done means before any code; tests written after implementation only confirm decisions.
Run features one at a time; parallel workers conflicted, duplicated work and burned tokens.
Put the right model in each seat; validation can use a different provider to avoid shared bias.
